definition: Hiding an otherwise-awkward discontinuous change (in the source example, an eye-direction change mid-turn) by making the changing element briefly not visible — e.g. closing the eyes — rather than attempting to animate the discontinuity smoothly.
purpose: Avoid having to smoothly animate a change that has no good continuous path (a redirected eye target mid-turn has no natural in-between), by removing the need for one instead.
visible_effect: The element in question (eyes, in the source example) is briefly hidden or closed at the exact moment its underlying value changes discontinuously, then reappears already at its new value.
psychological_or_gameplay_effect: The viewer never sees the discontinuity at all, so nothing needs to read as smooth — the concealment IS the solution, not a smoothing trick.
physical_interpretation: None — an authoring trick, not a physical model.
use_cases: an eye-direction or gaze-target change mid-turn, closing the eyes across the change (the source example)
generalizes to any hard-to-interpolate value change — a prop swap, a costume change, a rig retarget — hidden behind a blink, a fast pass, a hit-flash, or a brief occlusion
non_use_cases: a change the audience is specifically meant to see happen — this technique is for changes that would otherwise be a distracting or unconvincing pop
overusing the concealment itself to the point the blink, flash, or occlusion becomes its own distraction
interactions: Staging — this is a staging technique in miniature: controlling what the viewer is allowed to see, and when
Secondary action — closing the eyes IS itself a secondary action performing double duty as the concealment mechanism
cadence_representation: No representation, and Cadence is further from having one than the source medium: this build has no facial or eye rig concept at all (already named under `secondary_action` as out of scope for this Roblox-body-rig build), so even the specific source example has no Cadence equivalent yet — the GENERALIZED version (concealing any hard-to-interpolate change behind a visibility gap) is representable in principle through ordinary item visibility/property tracks, but nothing in this build authors or reasons about a "conceal the pop" plan.
control_surface: None directly; a generalized version would ride on ordinary property-track visibility toggling, which exists as a track type but is not driven by any planning tool for this purpose.
detection_and_measurement_methods: None — this build has no discontinuity-classification step that would ask "was this pop concealed by a visibility gap" versus "is this an unintended pop", the same open judgement `ai/motion.js classifyVariation` already states for other kinds of discontinuity.
failure_modes: a value change with no concealment at all, which reads as a visible, unintended pop
a concealment that is itself too long or too obvious, drawing exactly the attention it was meant to avoid
roblox_considerations: Directly usable once declared: a Roblox rig's visibility or transparency property is an ordinary animatable value, so the mechanism itself needs nothing engine-specific — only a Cadence-side facial/eye or prop-swap model to apply it to, which does not exist yet.
examples: Carl the raccoon's eyes closed at the start of his head turn specifically so his eye direction/target can change without an awkward mid-turn eye redraw (video @ 5:09–5:12)
evidence_status: video: https://youtu.be/thDT-4RjAeo @ 5:09–5:12 — stated directly and specifically in the transcript; no frame in this session's 9-frame sample falls near this timestamp (nearest are at 2:04 and 9:45); experimental until validated
